title: WHAT IF YOU COULD CATCH A STAR?

segments.line: Midnight in the park.
Freezing air, numb hands.
Above the trees, a bright
streak of light slashes across the dark.
You do not make a wish. You just reach up.
Catch. Time stutters.
The falling streak freezes right
in your open palm, humming
like a living ember. Warm
golden light spills between your mittens.
Soon your jars are glowing with starlight,
a queue stretches round the block,
sirens wail, and the clouds turn blood red.
What if you could catch a star?
Chapter One. The First Catch.
It starts on a quiet night in early November,
as the Northern Taurids build toward their peak
around November twelfth. You
are walking home through the park, breath misting
in the cold. A shooting star
flashes overhead. Just
for a laugh, you point your mitten at the sky
and close your fingers.
Catch. A soft
chime rings out. Down
drops a glowing golden pebble,
landing gently in your palm.
It does not burn. It feels
like a warm marshmallow.
You slip it into your pocket, and
the walk home feels like summer.
Back in your bedroom, you pluck another
streak through the window and drop it into an empty
jam jar on your nightstand. Instant
nightlight.
At your desk, a captured star
keeps your mug of cocoa piping hot while you work.
You think you have found the ultimate cosy life hack.
Until you look at the window and see your mate Mo staring
through the glass.
Wait. Those fall out of
the sky for free, and you are using them to warm
up cocoa?
Chapter Two. Wishes for Sale.
By the next evening, Mo has turned
your secret into a business. He
sets up a folding table by the park gate,
strings up lights, and tapes a cardboard
sign to the front: Genuine
Shooting Stars, Hold Your Own Wish.
You stand behind the table with empty mason
jars, plucking streaks out of the sky
on demand. Catch.
Catch. Each one
lands with a golden chime.
Step right up! Fresh
off the cosmos! Make a wish
while it is still warm, no refunds!
At first, it is silly fun.
A nervous teenager holds a glowing jar
and wishes to pass his driving test.
A kid wishes for a puppy.
Your pockets fill with cash, and the queue
stretches round the block.
Then the mood turns ugly.
People in fancy coats shove to the front,
waving money and demanding brighter stars.
Customers storm back, furious
that their selfish wishes have not come true.
Someone tries to smash a jar open on the path.
Inside the glass, the captured stars
pulse faster, humming with a low
vibration that makes your teeth ache.
Because what you are catching is not fairy dust at
all.
Chapter Three. The Real Science.
Let us pause the chaos and look at what a shooting
star really is. When you see
a streak of light in the night sky,
it is not a giant cartoon star.
It is a meteoroid. And most
visible meteors come from particles sand
grain to pebble sized. That is real.
Even weirder, they are nowhere near
the trees. Most meteors burn
up roughly eighty to one hundred and twenty
kilometres above the ground, high
in the mesosphere and lower thermosphere.
That is real.
So how can a tiny pebble eighty kilometres
up shine brightly enough to see from the park?
Speed. Taurid meteoroids
enter the atmosphere at about twenty seven
kilometres per second. That is real.
And at twenty seven kilometres per second,
the rock is not on fire like wood.
Instead, the air around the meteoroid
is heated and ionised into a glowing trail
of plasma. The glow is
mostly superheated air.
Catching a pebble at that speed should be completely
impossible.
Your power works by locking onto a meteoroid
from below and slowing it to a dead stop in your palm.
Which raises a big question.
Where does all that stopped energy go?
Into the jar. And what happens
when you reach for something bigger?
Chapter Four. Bigger Fish.
Alongside tiny dust grains,
the Taurids are famous for bright fireballs,
made by much larger chunks of rock.
Late that night, you climb onto the rooftop
above the city. Glowing jars
line the wall, humming in the dark.
Pebbles feel too small now.
You want a real prize.
Suddenly, a brilliant green and gold
fireball blazes across the clouds,
lighting up the whole street.
Mo grabs your sleeve.
Leave that one alone, mate!
Look at the trail on it!
That thing looks angry!
You reach up anyway. Catch.
The sky flashes white.
A shockwave rolls across the roof,
popping every bulb on the string lights.
The fireball slams to a stop above your
mittens, shrinking into a sputtering
core of blinding plasma.
Every car alarm on the street goes off.
Because when a bright fireball vanishes mid
flight on weather radar and satellite cameras,
the world notices.
By morning, news vans block your street,
scientists with sensors surround the park,
and government agents in dark suits knock
on your door. They are not here
to arrest you. Their telescopes
just spotted something else.
Chapter Five. Something Much
Bigger.
Inside a briefing room, the agents
turn a radar screen toward you.
Hidden inside the Taurid stream is a dark,
house sized object hurtling toward
Earth at twenty seven kilometres per second,
right on course for the city.
There is no time to evacuate, and
nothing else can stop it. So
the world asks you to stand in the park and catch it.
That night, the city cuts every
light. Searchlights sweep
the clouds. Scientists watch
from behind shields. Mo
stands beside you on the path, knees shaking.
No pressure or anything. Just
the whole city behind us. Use
both hands, yeah?
High above, roughly one hundred kilometres
up, the clouds turn blood red.
A deep roar shakes the ground as
a colossal fireball tears through the upper
air, dragging a tail of plasma
across the sky. You plant
your feet, raise both hands toward
the glare, and whisper the word.
Catch. A shockwave
flattens the grass. The roar
drops into silence.
Slowly, impossibly, the
giant fireball halts just above your fingertips.
And as the plasma clears, your breath catches.
Chapter Six. What You Caught.
The superheated air fades into the night
breeze, and you finally see what
is hovering above your palms. It
is not a jagged space rock.
Its surface is smooth dark metal,
shaped into clean geometric panels that glint
in the moonlight, etched with glowing cyan
symbols no human ever wrote.
Behind you, every mason jar
you filled all week suddenly flares bright
blue. All those tiny
pebbles pulse in the exact same rhythm,
answering the craft above your hands.
They were never random grains of space dust.
They were beacons, sent ahead to find someone who could catch them.
And now that you have caught their ship, a
hatch on its underside clicks open.
If you could catch a falling star tonight,
and it answered back, would you open your
hand, or let it go?
